one_liner: Header-only C++17 dynamic perfect-hash map/set with unordered_map-like API: lookups 1.2-7.6x faster than std::unordered_map, inserts far slower.
what_it_does: fph-table provides four containers (fph::DynamicFphMap/Set and fph::MetaFphMap/Set), each keeping a collision-free (perfect) hash over its current key set so find() inspects exactly one slot. The API follows std::unordered_map/set (find, contains, insert, emplace, try_emplace, erase, operator[], at, reserve, rehash, forward iterators, C++20-style heterogeneous lookup), with two differences: the hash parameter is a SeedHash functor called as (key, seed), and the Dynamic variants need a random-key generator for custom key types. Extra calls expose the structure: GetSlotPos() turns the table into a pure key-to-unique-index perfect hash, GetPointerNoCheck() does a compare-free lookup for keys known to be present, and InsertNoDuplicated() does bulk builds. A separate `noseed` branch takes ordinary std::hash-style functors, provided every inserted key hashes to a distinct value.
how_it_is_fast: It is derived from the FCH minimal-perfect-hash algorithm (Fox, Chen, Heath 1992): keys are grouped into about c*n/(log2 n + 1) buckets (default c = 2.0), and each bucket stores an offset plus one selector bit, found by a randomized seed search at build time, so that every key lands in a distinct power-of-two slot. A lookup is one seed hash, two multiply-and-shift steps with per-table random seeds, one read from the small bucket-parameter array (about 2 bits per key, so it stays in cache), and one slot read followed by a single key compare, with no probe loop. FPH drops FCH's two-step hash selection to remove a branch (paying for it with slower builds), and DynamicFph marks empty slots with a random 'filler' key instead of an occupancy bitmap, avoiding an extra memory load. MetaFph instead adds 1 byte of metadata per slot (7 hash bits plus a position marker), so most misses are rejected without touching the slot array.
when_to_use: Read-mostly or static key sets: build once with the range constructor, InsertNoDuplicated() or Build(), then run many find()/contains() calls, e.g. ID-to-record, symbol or routing tables.

64-bit integer keys with skewed or structured bit patterns. The default SimpleSeedHash is the identity for integers and the table mixes with random seeds itself. In the author's benchmark on keys where only ceil(log2 n) bits vary, it beat every std::unordered_map + hash pairing 2.1-7.6x on a Threadripper 3990X from n=32 to 10^7.
Tables of roughly 10^3 to 10^6 entries that fit in L2/L3. The author's 2023 rerun has DynamicFphMap fastest for hit lookups at 8,192 to 3.1M elements on Xeon E-2388G and 8,192 to 1.2M on M1 Max.
Lookup-bound code that only needs a key-to-unique-index mapping (GetSlotPos, which skips the slot fetch), or whose keys are guaranteed present (GetPointerNoCheck, no compare or branch).

Large tables with many failed lookups: use fph::MetaFphMap, whose metadata array rejects most misses without reading the slots. The 2023 rerun has it fastest for misses above 6,000 elements on Rocket Lake and above 200,000 on M1 Max.
when_not_to_use: Insert- or erase-heavy workloads. In the same benchmark CSVs on the 3990X, insert-with-reserve at n=10^7 cost about 2,517 ns per element vs 193 ns for std::unordered_map. Erase+insert at n=150,000 cost 2,176 ns vs 59 ns, and at 10^7 it timed out. An insert that breaks perfectness re-places its bucket or rebuilds the whole table.

Very small tables on x86 and very large hit-lookup tables at default load factor. ska::flat_hash_map + std::hash beat it below about 1,000 elements on the 3990X, and in the 2023 rerun again when data fit in L2 and once it exceeded L3. For large-n misses, absl::flat_hash_map beat DynamicFphMap in the 2022 data.

Key sets you cannot vet. If the seed search fails, which duplicate keys passed to Build()/InsertNoDuplicated() or poorly distributed hashes can cause, construction throws std::invalid_argument ('timeout when try to build fph map'), or calls std::abort with exceptions disabled. With 64-bit hashes of long keys (strings), the README warns collisions become likely beyond about 10^9 keys.
Code that needs std::unordered_map's reference stability, node handles (extract/merge), insert_or_assign, or stateful hashers and allocators. None of these are provided.

Maturity-sensitive deployments. The header logic has not changed since August 2023, the project has 55 stars, and its own CI docs admit an unfixed defect that trips an assert at -O0 and becomes heap corruption under -DNDEBUG, plus a known defect that crashes on x86-64 but passes on arm64. No issue describes either one.

integration.dependencies: none (standard library only); optional CMake INTERFACE target fph::fph_table via add_subdirectory
integration.min_toolchain: C++17. CI compiles with GCC and Clang at C++17/20/23 on Ubuntu 24.04 (GCC 13, Clang 18) and Apple clang on macOS 15. The README says MSVC compiles but it is not in CI. The published benchmarks used GCC 10.2 and Apple clang 13.1.6.
integration.platforms: Portable scalar C++ with no SIMD intrinsics. CI covers Linux x86-64, Linux arm64 and macOS arm64 (LP64). Windows/MSVC compiles per the README but is untested.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The const lookups (find/contains/count/GetSlotPos) only read table state. Any insert can relocate elements or rebuild the whole table, so writers need exclusive access.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — member names and semantics mostly match std::unordered_map, but the hash parameter must be a (key, seed) SeedHash (or use the noseed branch). Custom key types need a RandomKeyGenerator for the Dynamic variants, keys must be CopyConstructible, references are invalidated on rehash or rebuild, and there are no node handles and no insert_or_assign.

gotchas: The const operator[] on DynamicFphMap is noexcept and skips the key check (it calls GetPointerNoCheck). For an absent key it silently returns another element's value or reads an unconstructed slot. Use find() or at() unless the key is known to be present.

SeedHash and KeyEqual are static constexpr members, so they must be stateless and constexpr default-constructible, and a hasher instance passed to the constructor is ignored. Slot and bucket storage use default-constructed rebound allocators, so stateful allocators are not honored.

Empty slots in the Dynamic variants hold copies of a randomly generated filler key. Every unused slot therefore holds a constructed key (a random short string for std::string keys), and custom key types must supply a RandomKeyGenerator. MetaFph* avoids this with its metadata byte.

Pointers and references can be invalidated by any insert (bucket re-placement or full rebuild), not only by rehash. begin() moves to the most recently inserted or erased element, so iteration order shifts after every modification. The default max_load_factor is 0.6 (settable up to 0.98) over power-of-two slot counts, and the default BucketParamType=uint32_t caps capacity at 2^31 slots.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick fph-table over the constexpr-oriented siblings (constexpr-phf, ConstexprCore/perfect_hash) and frozen's small fixed tables when keys are only known at run time, number from thousands to millions, or need occasional insert/erase behind an unordered_map-style API. Pick it over cxxmph's mph_map for integer keys: fph reports 2-7x over std::unordered_map, while cxxmph claims 10-50% on large URL-string sets.
verified_claims_summary: The author's own hashtable-bench (January 2022 snapshot) measured average ns per hit find() in a throughput loop on uint64 keys where only ceil(log2 n) bits vary, with tables rehashed at max_load_factor 0.9 and n from 32 to 10^7. DynamicFphMap + SimpleSeedHash took 2.04-30.98 ns vs 10.53-66.43 ns for std::unordered_map + std::hash on a Threadripper 3990X (GCC 10.2, libstdc++, Release -O3), 2.1-7.6x faster than the best std::unordered_map pairing; on an M1 Max (Apple clang 13.1.6, libc++, -mcpu=native) it took 1.63-14.79 ns vs 2.43-45.01 ns for the best pairing (robin_hood::hash), 1.2-7.3x, while libc++ std::unordered_map + std::hash timed out on this dataset at larger sizes.
status_note: Header logic frozen since August 2023, but the author added an Apache-2.0 license and an extensive CI suite (compile matrix, ctest, ASan/UBSan, asm/callgrind lookup gates) in August 2026, so it is lightly maintained, and at two self-contained headers of about 4k lines each it is easy to vendor and pin.
